solution:
Anode (left) is the \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode, cathode (right) the hydrogen electrode :

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)  (oxidation)

\(2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)  (reduction)

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0(\text{cathode}) - E^0(\text{anode}) = 0 - (-0.76\ \mathrm{V}) = 0.76\ \mathrm{V}\)

Because \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is a gas its concentration term is replaced by its partial pressure :

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}]\,P_{\mathrm{H_2}}}{[\mathrm{H^\oplus}]^2}\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}\dfrac{0.2 \times 1.8}{(1.6)^2}\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}(0.1406)\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times (-0.8520) = 0.76\ \mathrm{V} + 0.0252\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= 0.785\ \mathrm{V}\)

(\(E^0_{Zn} = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}\) is taken from Table 5.1 of the chapter.)

[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working substitutes \(\Lambda_c = 16.6\) where its own stem states 16.5 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). The printed result 0.0422 follows from 16.5 (16.5/390.7 = 0.0422, whereas 16.6/390.7 = 0.0425), so the stem and the final answer agree with each other and only the substituted value was wrong. The line has been corrected to 16.5; the answers 0.0422 and \(1.86 \times 10^{-5}\) are unaffected.]

The degree of dissociation,

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_c}{\Lambda_0} = \dfrac{16.5\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}}{390.7\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0422\)

\(K_a = \dfrac{\alpha^2 c}{1 - \alpha} = \dfrac{(0.0422)^2 \times 0.01}{(1 - 0.0422)} = 1.86 \times 10^{-5}\)
note: 0.0422^2 x 0.01 / 0.9578 = 1.859e-5, printed 1.85e-5 (also in the note above).

[Textbook misprint: the book prints the reversed equation (iv) first as \(\Delta_r H^0 = -911\) kJ and then, four lines later, correctly as \(+911\) kJ. Reversing equation (i) must flip the sign, so \(+911\) kJ is right and the first printing is a misprint; it has been corrected here. Note also that the three values summed give \(-221 - 65.3 + 911 = +624.7\) kJ, which the book rounds to \(+624\) kJ.]

Reverse the Eq. (i)
iv. \(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) \longrightarrow Si(s) + O_2(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Add equations (ii), (iii) and (iv)
ii. \(\mathrm{2\,C(graphite) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,CO(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -221\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
iii. \(\mathrm{Si(s) + C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -65.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
iv. \(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) \longrightarrow Si(s) + O_2(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

\(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) + 3\,C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s) + 2\,CO(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +624.7\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
note: The sum is +624.7 kJ (the note above says so); the answer line printed the book's +624.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working ends "\(= 4955\ \mathrm{J} = 4.955\ \mathrm{J}\)", a false equality: 4955 J is 4.955 kJ, not 4.955 J. The unit has been corrected here; the value 4955 J and the conclusion that work is done on the system are as printed.]

For oxidation of 4 moles of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), the reaction is
\(\mathrm{4\,SO_2(g) + 2\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow 4\,SO_3(g)}\)
\(W = -\Delta n_g RT\)
\(\Delta n_g = 4 - 6 = -2\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
Hence,
\(W = -(-2\ \mathrm{mol}) \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= 4955\ \mathrm{J} = 4.955\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Work is done on the system (since \(W > 0\)).
note: The minus belongs to Delta n = -2 mol, not to R; W = +4955 J unchanged.

solution:
The expansion is isothermal and reversible, so
\(W_{max} = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\)

Molar mass of \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(n = \dfrac{24\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.75\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\), \(P_1 = 1.6\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(P_2 = 1\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(W_{max} = -2.303 \times 0.75\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} \dfrac{1.6}{1}\)
\(= -2.303 \times 0.75 \times 8.314 \times 298 \times 0.20412\)
\(= -873.5\ \mathrm{J}\)

The maximum work is \(-873.5\ \mathrm{J}\) (about \(-0.87\) kJ). The negative sign shows the work is done BY the gas on the surroundings, as expected for an expansion.
note: -873.5 J needs log 1.6 = 0.20412; with 0.2041 the line gives -873.4.

[Textbook misprint: the working establishes \(1222.56 = M_2' \times 18.173\) and then divides by 18.175 on the next line. The two differ in the last digit only and both give \(M_2' = 67.3\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), so the answer is unaffected and the printed values are preserved below.]

| | Urea | Unknown compound |
|---|---|---|
| mass of solute | \(\mathrm{W_2} = 1.02\) g | \(\mathrm{W_2}' = 1.609\) g |
| mass of solvent | \(\mathrm{W_1} = 98.5\) g | \(\mathrm{W_1}' = 86\) g |
| freezing point depression | \(\Delta T_f = 0.211\) K | \(\Delta T_f' = 0.34\) K |
| molar mass | \(M_2 = 60\) \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) | \(M_2' = ?\) |

\(1000K_f = \dfrac{M_2 \times \Delta T_f \times \mathrm{W_1}}{\mathrm{W_2}} = \dfrac{M_2' \times \Delta T_f' \times \mathrm{W_1}'}{\mathrm{W_2}'}\)

\(= \dfrac{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.211\ \mathrm{K} \times 98.5\ \mathrm{g}}{1.02\ \mathrm{g}} = \dfrac{M_2' \times 0.34\ \mathrm{K} \times 86\ \mathrm{g}}{1.609\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(\dfrac{1247.01\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}}}{1.02} = \dfrac{M_2' \times 29.24\ \mathrm{K}}{1.609}\)

\(1222.56\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}} = M_2' \times 18.173\)

\(M_2' = \dfrac{1222.56\ \mathrm{g\ K\ mol^{-1}}}{18.175\ \mathrm{K}} = 67.3\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)
note: 1247.01 / 1.02 = 1222.56, printed 1222.55 (3 places); the noted 18.175 and the answer 67.3 stand.

solution:
Both solutes are nonelectrolytes, so \(\Delta T_f = K_fm\) and, for the same solvent, \(\Delta T_f\) is proportional to the molality alone.

A 5% solution by mass contains 5 g of solute in 95 g of water, that is 0.095 kg of water.

Cane sugar, \(M = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(m_{\text{sugar}} = \dfrac{5/342}{0.095} = 0.15389\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Glucose, \(M = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(m_{\text{glucose}} = \dfrac{5/180}{0.095} = 0.29240\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

For the sugar solution, taking the freezing point of pure water as 273.15 K,

\(\Delta T_f(\text{sugar}) = 273.15\ \mathrm{K} - 271\ \mathrm{K} = 2.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

Since \(\Delta T_f \propto m\),

\(\Delta T_f(\text{glucose}) = 2.15\ \mathrm{K} \times \dfrac{0.29240}{0.15389} = 2.15 \times \dfrac{342}{180} = 4.085\ \mathrm{K}\)

(The ratio of the molalities is simply the inverse ratio of the molar masses, \(342/180 = 1.9\), because the two solutions contain equal masses of solute in equal masses of water.)

Therefore the freezing point of the 5% glucose solution is

\(T_f = 273.15\ \mathrm{K} - 4.085\ \mathrm{K} = 269.07\ \mathrm{K}\)

The cell contents are isotonic with 0.3 M sugar, and sugar does not dissociate, so the osmotic pressure INSIDE the cell is

\(\pi_{\text{in}} = MRT = 0.3 \times 0.0821 \times 310 = 7.64\ \mathrm{atm}\)

KCl dissociates completely into \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), so \(i = 2\) and the OUTSIDE solution exerts

\(\pi_{\text{out}} = iMRT = 2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0821 \times 310 = 5.09\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The outside solution is therefore hypotonic to the cell, solvent enters the cell, and the osmotic pressure that develops across the membrane is the difference

\(\pi = 7.64 - 5.09 = 2.55\ \mathrm{atm}\) (2.545 before rounding, which is option (B), 2.54 atm)

Why the other options fail: 5.08 atm is \(\pi_{\text{out}}\) alone, which is a property the KCl solution already had before the cell was placed in it and would leave the whole first sentence of the question unused; 4.92 atm and 2.46 atm are the same two quantities evaluated at 300 K instead of body temperature, 310 K.

[Note: the four printed options are degenerate, because \(0.3 - 0.2 = 0.1\) and \(0.3 - 0.1 = 0.2\), the same four numbers arise whether one computes the osmotic pressure of the KCl solution or the difference across the membrane, so the option set alone cannot settle the reading. This answer takes "what osmotic pressure DEVELOPS when the cell is placed in the solution" as the pressure arising across the membrane, which is the only reading that uses the given 0.3 M sugar data. A student who answered 5.08 atm has computed \(\pi_{\text{out}}\) correctly, including the van't Hoff factor.]
note: 7.64 - 5.09 = 2.55, printed 2.54; unrounded 2.545, keyed option B 2.54 stands.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed working gives \(255.1/32 = 7.92\); the division is 7.97. The conclusion is unaffected, since both round to 8 and the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{S_8}\), so the printed value is preserved below. The stem also opens a parenthesis before "Given that" which is never closed.]

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\mathrm{W_1} = 100\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_2} = 3.795\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\Delta T_b = (319.81 - 319.45)\ \mathrm{K} = 0.36\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{g\ kg^{-1}} \times 2.42\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 3.795\ \mathrm{g}}{0.36\ \mathrm{K} \times 100\ \mathrm{g}} = 255.11\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Atomic mass of S = 32 u

Therefore number of atoms in a molecule of sulphur

\(= \dfrac{\text{molar mass of S}}{\text{atomic mass of S}} = \dfrac{255.1}{32} = 7.97 \approx 8\)

The molecular formula would be \(\mathrm{S_8}\) in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\)
note: 1000 x 2.42 x 3.795 / 36 = 255.108 -> 255.11; 255.1/32 = 7.97 (the printed working's 7.92, noted above, corrected in the line).

solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints (16.17 mm Hg). Raoult's law gives \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1 = 17 \times 2.7778/(2.7778 + 0.04667) = 16.72\) mm Hg for 2.8 g of urea (60 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) in 50 g of water, and the dilute-solution approximation gives 16.71 mm Hg, the same to three significant figures. The printed value would require about 8.6 g of urea, and appears to be 16.71 with its last two digits transposed.]

Urea is a nonvolatile, nonionizing solute, so Raoult's law gives the vapour pressure of the solution as \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\), where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of water.

Moles of urea (molar mass 60 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)):

\(n_2 = \dfrac{2.8\ \mathrm{g}}{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.04667\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Moles of water (molar mass 18 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)):

\(n_1 = \dfrac{50\ \mathrm{g}}{18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2.7778\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Mole fraction of water:

\(x_1 = \dfrac{n_1}{n_1 + n_2} = \dfrac{2.7778}{2.7778 + 0.04667} = \dfrac{2.7778}{2.8245} = 0.98348\)

Hence

\(P_1 = P_1^0x_1 = 17\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.98348 = 16.72\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

The vapour pressure of the solution is 16.72 mm Hg, a lowering of 0.28 mm Hg. (Using the dilute-solution approximation \(\Delta P/P_1^0 = n_2/n_1\) instead gives 16.71 mm Hg, the same value to three significant figures.)
